summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of atrial fibrillation, systolic heart failure (EF 30%), diabetes, obesity, and recent stroke was admitted for intermittent left-sided chest pain that began the morning of admission. The pain was dull, associated with nausea, worsened by movement and lying down, and partially attributed to muscle strain after heavy lifting and possible GERD from a spicy meal. Initial evaluation showed no acute myocardial infarction on EKG, but troponins trended slightly upward before declining, suggesting demand ischemia. Elevated BNP and chest X-ray findings indicated acute on chronic heart failure exacerbation due to volume overload, likely from dietary indiscretion. He was treated with intravenous and oral diuretics, resulting in significant fluid loss and symptom improvement. Hypokalemia triggered episodes of ventricular tachycardia, which resolved with potassium repletion. His atrial fibrillation remained rate-controlled, and INR was therapeutic. Chest pain resolved with morphine and supportive care. Medications were adjusted at discharge, including increased metoprolol and aspirin, short-term increased Lasix, and potassium supplementation. A sleep clinic follow-up was arranged to address obstructive sleep apnea and pulmonary hypertension.
